# Conclusion
This paper contributes to the literature on market anomalies by testing Propositions 1 and 2 from Frazzini and Pedersen (2014) [@frazzinipedersen2014], which seek to explain the beta anomaly and the performance of the BAB strategy. Using data from US equity markets we find evidence of a negative relationship between beta and alpha, supporting Proposition 1 and confirming that the empirical Security Market Line is significantly flatter than CAPM predicts. We also find that the BAB portfolio generates positive returns, supporting Proposition 2. However, when we introduce transaction costs, the performance of the BAB portfolio is significantly reduced under the assumption of full monthly rebalancing using CRSP quoted spreads — an estimate that almost certainly represents an upper bound on true implementation costs, as argued by Frazzini, Israel, and Moskowitz [@frazziniisraelmoskowitz2015].

The limitations of this paper include the focus on US equity markets, which may limit the generalisability of our findings, and the use of quoted bid-ask spreads rather than effective spreads or actual execution data to measure transaction costs. Future research could address these limitations by extending the analysis to international markets and asset classes, by applying effective spread estimates or execution data as in Frazzini, Israel, and Moskowitz [@frazziniisraelmoskowitz2015], and by conducting sub-period analyses to assess whether the anomaly has weakened following its publication and the growth of factor investing. A further avenue would be to assess whether BAB returns survive risk adjustment under richer factor models such as those of Carhart [@carhart1997] and Fama and French [@famafrench2015].
